## Source and scope

Anthropic’s **“Effective harnesses for long-running agents,”** written by Justin Young and published on November 26, 2025, describes experiments with Claude doing software-development work across multiple context windows.

**The article does not document one complete failed run.** It reports recurring behavior across experiments, uses a **claude.ai clone** as its principal example, and supplies an abbreviated session opening from the subsequently revised setup. The chronology below distinguishes those observations rather than combining them into an invented single trajectory.

## 1. Claude was asked to build a substantial web application

The article describes **Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows**, with a high-level request such as:

> “build a clone of claude.ai.”

The expected result was a production-quality web application, not merely a partial interface or a few working interactions.

The SDK provided tools and context-management capabilities, including compaction. However, work continued across discrete sessions, and a new session did not inherently remember everything the preceding session had done. Claude therefore had to recover the project’s state from the context and artifacts available to it.

The article does not provide the complete original prompt, repository, implementation transcript, or numbered sequence of failing sessions.

## 2. In early work, Claude attempted much of the application at once

The researchers report that Claude tended to attempt to “one-shot the app,” undertaking too much implementation within a single session.

Frequently, Claude ran out of context while implementation was still underway. The state left behind included **a feature that was only partly implemented and insufficiently documented**.

When a subsequent session began, Claude had to inspect that unfinished work and infer what the preceding session had been doing. The article says the agent would:

> “have to guess at what had happened, and spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again.”

This occurred even with compaction enabled; the information passed into the next session was not always sufficiently clear.

No specific edit commands, affected files, runtime errors, or compaction outputs are shown for these episodes. The observable sequence reported by the authors is: broad implementation work, interruption at the context boundary, an incomplete handoff, and substantial reconstruction or repair work in the next session.

## 3. Later sessions sometimes announced completion while work remained

The article separately describes behavior that often occurred later in a project, after some features had been implemented.

A fresh Claude instance would inspect the application, recognize that progress had been made, and **declare the overall job finished**. The authors describe these declarations as occurring too early, before the requested application was complete.

The article does not reproduce one of these final messages, identify exactly which requirements were still missing, or show a user or evaluator correcting the declaration. It also does not establish that this happened in the same run as any particular context-exhaustion episode.

Thus, what the source supports is a repeated observation: later sessions sometimes treated an already partially implemented application as a completed assignment.

## 4. Individual features were also marked complete without working end to end

During implementation, Claude sometimes made code changes and performed limited checks, including:

- Running unit tests.
- Using `curl` against a development server.

Despite those checks, the researchers observed Claude marking features complete when they did not work through the full user interaction.

The article states that Claude would:

> “fail [to] recognize that the feature didn’t work end-to-end.”

It does not supply the corresponding unit-test output, HTTP responses, exact `curl` commands, or a specific broken feature from these episodes. Consequently, the source does **not** establish that any particular test suite passed or that a particular server response falsely indicated success. It establishes that the checks Claude performed did not lead it to recognize the remaining end-to-end problem before recording completion.

## 5. The researchers changed what the first and subsequent sessions were asked to do

After describing these observations, the article reports a revised setup.

The first session was given an initialization-specific prompt asking Claude to create:

- An `init.sh` startup script.
- A `claude-progress.txt` record of work.
- An initial Git commit.
- A comprehensive feature-requirements file.

For the claude.ai-clone example, the requirements file contained **more than 200 features**, all initially marked as failing. One example described creating a new conversation and checking the resulting chat area and sidebar entry; its JSON record ended with `"passes": false`.

Subsequent coding sessions were instructed to work on **one feature at a time**, update progress notes, and commit their work with descriptive messages. They were instructed to change only the requirements’ completion status, not remove or rewrite the tests.

The article notes that the initializer and coding agents were distinguished by their initial user prompts. Their system prompt, tools, and overall harness were otherwise identical.

The researchers report that Git history and progress notes helped later sessions understand prior work and recover working code states, reducing time spent reconstructing what had happened.

## 6. Claude was explicitly directed to test through the browser

The researchers also instructed Claude to use browser automation and test the application as a human user would.

With the **Puppeteer MCP server**, Claude could interact with the application and inspect screenshots. The article includes an animation captioned as screenshots Claude took while testing the clone. The authors report that these interactions enabled Claude to identify and fix bugs that were not apparent from code inspection alone.

Some problems remained. Specifically, Claude could not see **browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP interface**. The researchers observed that features relying on those modals tended to be buggier.

The article does not provide an individual modal-related interaction, its tool response, or the subsequent completion decision.

## 7. The only displayed session sequence comes from the revised setup

The article then shows what it calls a “typical” session opening. In its abbreviated tool notation, Claude:

1. Announces that it will determine the project’s current state.
2. Runs `bash - pwd`.
3. Reads `claude-progress.txt`.
4. Reads `feature_list.json`.
5. Runs `bash - git log --oneline -20`.
6. Checks for an `init.sh` script.
7. Starts the development server.
8. Navigates to the application and tests existing functionality.

For the clone, the surrounding text describes the basic browser check as starting a new chat, sending a message, and receiving a response.

In the displayed example, Claude then reports:

> “The core chat features, theme switching, conversation loading, and error handling are all functioning correctly.”

It says it will review `tests.json` more comprehensively to determine what to implement next, and the excerpt ends with a placeholder indicating that work on a new feature begins.

**This is not a fully inspectable verification trace.** Server startup and browser testing appear as placeholders, without exact commands, browser-tool arguments, or returned results. The statement that the features work is Claude’s report within that example.

## Final reported outcome

For the original setup, the article reports that a high-level prompt plus repeated SDK sessions was insufficient to reliably produce a production-quality application. Work could be left unfinished and undocumented, subsequent sessions spent time restoring basic functionality, and Claude sometimes declared either features or the entire project complete before they actually were.

For the revised setup, the authors report better incremental progress, clearer handoffs, and improved detection and repair of application bugs through browser testing. They still report unresolved testing limitations.

The article **does not provide a final acceptance-test result for a particular failed run, demonstrate that every feature of the clone ultimately passed, or quantify the improvement with completion rates**. Its endpoint is a qualitative account of the observed behavior and the results of changing the session instructions and working environment—not a complete, individually documented failure-and-recovery trajectory.

### Sources
- [Anthropic — Effective harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)

Justin Young’s Anthropic engineering article, dated November 26, 2025, describes a workflow for software agents operating over successive context windows. The account primarily reports **aggregate experimental observations**, with one illustrative session sequence—not a complete, individually documented execution trace.

### 1. Initial setup and observed failures

Long-duration tasks suffer from discontinuity: later sessions lack earlier sessions’ working context. The article compares this to developers handing a project between shifts without remembering preceding work.

Context compaction alone did not solve this. In experiments, Opus 4.5 using the Claude Agent SDK could not reliably produce a production-ready application from a broad request such as “build a clone of claude.ai”.

Two recurring problems appeared:

- **Excessive scope:** the agent attempted much of the application simultaneously, exhausted its context, and left incomplete functionality without adequate documentation. Subsequent sessions had to reconstruct intent and repair the application.
- **Early completion claims:** after observing some implemented functionality, later sessions sometimes incorrectly treated the overall assignment as finished.

The proposed remedy combined initial project preparation with small, verifiable increments and durable handoff records.

A setup-focused agent created:

- A startup script, “init.sh”.
- A persistent activity record, “claude-progress.txt”.
- An initial Git commit documenting the starting files.
- A comprehensive, structured requirements checklist.

The two agent roles differed only in their opening user instructions; their system instructions, tools, and surrounding infrastructure were otherwise unchanged.

For the chat-application example, the checklist contained more than 200 requirements, all initially unsuccessful.

12	Agents still face challenges working across many context windows. We looked to human engineers for inspiration in creating a more effective harness for long-running agents.
13	As AI agents become more capable, developers are increasingly asking them to take on complex tasks requiring work that spans hours, or even days. However, getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem.
14	The core challenge of long-running agents is that they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. Imagine a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift. Because context windows are limited, and because most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a way to bridge the gap between coding sessions.
15	We developed a two-fold solution to enable the Claude Agent SDK to work effectively across many context windows: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session, while leaving clear artifacts for the next session. You can find code examples in the accompanying quickstart.
